title: The crown of thorns (Mark 15:16–32)
hookLine: soldiers mock; Simon of Cyrene carries the cross; passers-by jeer

lines: PURPLE, AND A CROWN OF THORNS.
cards: The soldiers lead Jesus into the governor's courtyard and call together the whole company. Then they put on a show. They dress him in purple, twist a crown out of thorns and press it on his head.

They salute him: hail, King of the Jews! They strike his head with a reed, spit on him, and kneel in mock worship. It's the kind of cruelty bored, powerful people invent when someone can't fight back.
Then they strip off the purple, put his own clothes back on him, and lead him out to crucify him.

teach.h: SIMON OF CYRENE CARRIES THE CROSS.
teach.b: On the road out of the city, the soldiers grab a man coming in from the country, Simon of Cyrene, and make him carry the cross. Mark adds a detail nobody needed: Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus.
Why name the sons? Mark doesn't say; some readers think his first audience knew the family. A stranger pressed into service, and his name kept.

teach.h: GOLGOTHA: THE PLACE OF A SKULL.
teach.b: They come to Golgotha, which Mark translates: the place of a skull. They offer him wine mixed with myrrh, and he doesn't take it. They crucify him and divide his clothes by casting lots.

teach.h: THE CHARGE: THE KING OF THE JEWS.
teach.b: Above his head, the charge: the King of the Jews. Two bandits are crucified with him, one on each side. Then the mocking starts again, from everyone.

People walking past shake their heads: you who would destroy the temple, save yourself! The chief priests and scribes say to each other, in the King James Bible: "He saved others; himself he cannot save."
Even the men crucified beside him join in.
The strange thing is that the mockers keep saying things that, to Mark's readers, are true. They call him king in mockery; Christians call him king.
They say he saved others; Mark has spent the whole gospel showing just that: a leper, a little girl, a man in the tombs. And himself he cannot save is, for Christians, close to the whole point.
As Christians tell it, he doesn't come down, not because he can't, but because saving others is what he's doing. The mockers get the words right and the meaning upside down.

how: Some Christians, especially Catholics and Anglicans, walk the Stations of the Cross, especially on Fridays in Lent, stopping to remember moments like the crown of thorns and Simon of Cyrene carrying the cross.

games.q: you're Simon, coming in from the country. soldiers stop you and point at a cross. what happens?
o: you offer to take his place.
games.why: they compel Simon to carry the cross. Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus, as if the readers knew the family.

practice: Think of someone who's the butt of the joke right now, a kid at school, a coworker everyone rolls their eyes at, a stranger online, and picture their face.

Then picture Simon, who happened to be walking by and ended up carrying the weight, and what walking alongside that person might look like: one kind word, one seat next to them. If you pray, you can hold them before God.

wordCard.voice: Golgotha, which Mark translates for us: the place of a skull, where the mocking went on after the crown of thorns.
